subject: English
stem: When the stranger saw me, (a) / he seemed to recognise me (b) / and asked me what was my name. (c) / No error (d)
optC: and asked me what was my name.
solution: A question reported inside another clause is an indirect question, and an indirect question takes ordinary statement order, not the inverted order of a direct question. The direct form 'What was my name?' becomes 'what my name was' once it is reported after 'asked me'. Corrected sentence: When the stranger saw me, he seemed to recognise me and asked me what my name was. The fault lies in the third segment. Matches option C.

subject: English
stem: I and Gopal (a) / went to the meeting (b) / together. (c) / No error (d)
solution: When the speaker is one of two subjects joined by 'and', convention places the first person pronoun last, so the order should be the other person followed by 'I'. Corrected sentence: Gopal and I went to the meeting together. The fault lies in the first segment. Matches option A.

solution: The main clause is in the past tense, 'I did not know'. The leaving of the handbag happened before that knowing, so the subordinate clause needs the past perfect and not the present perfect. Corrected sentence: I did not know that you had left your handbag in our office when you came to see me last Friday. The fault lies in the second segment. Matches option B.

solution: The sentence states a general truth and opens in the present tense with 'wishes'. Both halves of the contrast must stay in the same tense, so the past form 'wanted' is out of place. Corrected sentence: Every man in this world wishes to live long but nobody wants to grow old. The fault lies in the third segment. Matches option C.

subject: English
stem: Neither of the scout leaders know (a) / how to trap wild animals (b) / or how to prepare them for mounting. (c) / No error (d)

optC: or how to prepare them for mounting.
solution: 'Neither of' is a singular pronoun and takes a singular verb, even though the noun that follows 'of' is plural. So 'Neither of the scout leaders know' must become 'Neither of the scout leaders knows'. Corrected sentence: Neither of the scout leaders knows how to trap wild animals or how to prepare them for mounting. The fault lies in the first segment. Matches option A.

subject: English

solution: 'Between' is used when exactly two things are involved and 'among' when there are more than two. Only two countries are spoken of here, so 'among the two countries' is wrong. Corrected sentence: The main purpose of the visit is to develop close relationship between the two countries. The fault lies in the third segment. Matches option C.

subject: English
stem: Had I been (a) / in my brothers position (b) / I would have refused the offer. (c) / No error (d)

solution: A noun that shows possession needs an apostrophe. The position spoken of belongs to the brother, so the possessive form 'brother's position' is required. Corrected sentence: Had I been in my brother's position I would have refused the offer. The fault lies in the second segment. Matches option B.

subject: English
stem: She does not listen to me. (a) / because she is (b) / senior than me (c) / No error (d)

solution: Adjectives taken from Latin comparatives, such as senior, junior, superior, inferior and prior, are followed by 'to' and never by 'than'. Corrected sentence: She does not listen to me because she is senior to me. The fault lies in the third segment. Matches option C.

subject: English
stem: One (a) / should keep (b) / his word. (c) / No error (d)
solution: When the indefinite pronoun 'one' is the subject, the possessive that refers back to it must also be a form of 'one'. Mixing it with 'his' breaks the agreement. Corrected sentence: One should keep one's word. The fault lies in the third segment. Matches option C.

solution: A definition begins with the thing being defined, so the subject and verb 'a web search engine is' must come first. The complement that defines it follows, and it is split into the tool and its purpose. The last part is an adjective phrase describing 'information', so it must sit next to that word. subject: History

stem: After which event did the British acquire the Diwani of Bengal, Bihar and Odisha?
solution: The Diwani, the right to collect the revenues of Bengal, Bihar and Odisha, was granted to the Company by the Mughal emperor Shah Alam the Second under the Treaty of Allahabad in 1765, and that treaty was the direct result of the Company's victory at Buxar in 1764 over the combined forces of the Nawab of Awadh, the deposed Nawab of Bengal and the emperor himself. Plassey in 1757 gave the Company control over the Nawab of Bengal but no revenue right, while the Regulating Act and Pitt's India Act were later measures by which Parliament in Britain took charge of the Company's affairs. Matches option B.

solution: The Palaiyakkarars, anglicised as Poligars, were the military chieftains who held territory in the Tamil country as feudatories of earlier rulers. The rising of 1799 centred on the fort of Panchalankurichi in the Tirunelveli region under Veerapandiya Kattabomman, who refused to pay tribute to the Company, so it took place in what is now Tamil Nadu. Matches option A.

subject: History

stem:
Consider the following statements:
1. The first to start a joint-stock company to trade with India were the Dutch.
2. In India, the Dutch established their earliest factory at Pulicat.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
solution: The second statement is wrong. The Dutch opened their earliest factory in India at Masulipatnam on the Andhra coast in 1605; Pulicat, where they raised Fort Geldria, was occupied only in 1610, and although it later became their chief settlement and mint in India it was not the first. The first statement stands, since the Dutch East India Company, chartered in 1602 with a permanent joint capital subscribed by shareholders, was the first joint-stock company formed for the eastern trade. So only the first statement is correct. Matches option A.
reviewNote: Rule 1: the two numbered statements are flattened into one line. Derivation: (1) the standard exam position is that the Dutch VOC (1602) was the first true joint-stock company trading with India, the English EIC having traded on terminable per-voyage stock until 1657 - accepted as true; (2) the Dutch first factory in India was Masulipatnam (1605), Pulicat came later (Fort Geldria 1613) - false. So only (1) = A, agreeing with the key.

1. There are 4 major and 25 minor seaports in India.
2. The major ports are under the administrative control of the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways.
3. The minor ports are under the jurisdiction of the respective State Maritime Board/State Government.

solution: Statement 1 is false. India has 12 major ports, not 4, and roughly 200 non-major (minor) ports rather than 25. Statement 2 is true: the major ports are administered by the Union government through the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways, under the Major Port Authorities Act. subject: Geography
chapter: Earth's Structure, Landforms and Geological Time
stem: Which of the following statements regarding volcanoes is not correct?
optA: Composite volcanoes erupt with loud explosions and rapid flow of lava.
optB: Volcano is the result of a hotspot underneath the Earth’s crust.
optC: They are generally formed at any plate boundary.
optD: Composite volcanoes are usually found at destructive plate boundaries.
solution: Volcanic activity is confined to particular kinds of plate margin. Where plates move apart, magma rises to fill the gap, and where one plate is forced down beneath another it melts and feeds volcanoes above. But where two plates simply slide past one another along a transform margin, as along the San Andreas fault, no magma is generated and no volcanoes are formed. It is therefore not true that volcanoes are formed at any plate boundary. Composite cones do lie along destructive margins, and a rising plume of hot material beneath the crust is a genuine additional source of volcanoes far from any plate edge, as under Hawaii. Matches option C.
reviewNote: Key C accepted: volcanism occurs at divergent and convergent boundaries but NOT at conservative/transform boundaries, so "generally formed at any plate boundary" is the incorrect statement. Note that options (A) ("rapid flow of lava" - composite-cone lava is viscous and slow) and (B) (hotspots explain only some volcanoes) are also loosely worded; C is nevertheless the clearly intended and most-wrong option. [blind derivation agrees with the printed key but at LOW confidence: The question is loosely built and more than one statement can be faulted. The description of composite volcanoes as producing a rapid flow of lava is also inaccurate, since their lava is andesitic and viscous and moves slowly, which is why the cones are steep; and the hotspot statement is true only of some volcanoes, not of volcanoes in general. I chose the plate-boundary statement because its error is unqualified and standard. This row should be checked by hand.]

subject: Biology
stem: Which of the following is a defining characteristic of living organisms?
solution: Growth cannot define life, because non-living things such as a mound of sand or a crystal in solution also increase in size, and because growth in living things is from within by cell division rather than by addition from outside. Reproduction cannot define it either, since sterile worker bees, mules and many barren individuals do not reproduce yet are unquestionably alive. Making sound is true of only a few animals and of no plant or microbe. What holds without exception is that every organism, from a bacterium turning towards a nutrient to a mammal reacting to light or heat, senses its surroundings and responds to them, and this ability is taken as the defining property of the living. Matches option D.
reviewNote: Filing is a compromise - no chapter covers "The Living World / characteristics of life"; Cell Structure Fundamentals is the closest general-biology home. Answer D follows NCERT XI: consciousness, the ability to sense and respond to environmental stimuli, is the defining property of living organisms.

subject: Chemistry
stem:
Which of the following are not chemical changes?
1. Tempering of iron
2. Conversion of the iron piece into an electro- magnet by passing the current around the iron.
3. Melting of iron
4. Rusting of iron Select the correct answer using the code given below:
solution: A chemical change produces a new substance with new properties and is not easily reversed. Tempering is a heat treatment that alters the hardness and internal structure of the metal while leaving it iron throughout. Magnetising a piece of iron by passing a current around it only aligns the magnetic domains already present in the metal, and the effect can be undone. Melting turns solid iron into liquid iron, a change of state alone, and cooling restores it. Only rusting forms a genuinely new substance, hydrated iron oxide, so the first three are not chemical changes and the fourth is. Matches option C.
reviewNote: Rule 1: the four numbered items and the code line are flattened into one line. Derivation: tempering (heat treatment), magnetisation and melting are physical; only rusting is chemical, so the non-chemical set is 1,2,3 = C.

subject: Chemistry
stem: Which of the following is a chemical change?
optA: Evaporation of sea water to get salt
solution: Burning methane in air turns it into carbon dioxide and water, substances quite different from the gas that was burnt, and no ordinary means will give the methane back, so the change is chemical. Evaporating sea water leaves the salt that was dissolved in it, camphor that sublimes can be condensed back to solid camphor, and sugar stirred into coffee can be recovered by evaporating the liquid. In each of those three the substance survives unchanged, so they are physical changes. Matches option B.

subject: Geography
stem:
Consider the following statements:
Statement 1: The temperature decreases with an increase in altitude.
Statement 2: The air density in the atmosphere decreases with height.
Which one of the following is correct in respect of the above statements?
optA: Both Statement 1 and Statement 2 are correct, and Statement 2 is the correct explanation for Statement 1.
optB: Both Statement 1 and Statement 2 are correct, but Statement 2 is not the correct explanation for Statement 1.
optC: Statement 1 is correct, but Statement 2 is not correct.
optD: Statement 1 is not correct, but Statement 2 is correct.
solution: Both statements are true. Through the troposphere, the lowest layer and the one in which weather occurs, temperature falls at an average of about 6.5 degrees Celsius for every kilometre climbed. Air density also falls steadily with height, because the air near the surface is compressed by the weight of all the air above it while there is little weight above the upper layers. The second is a genuine reason for the first. The atmosphere is warmed not directly by the sun but from below, by the long wave radiation given out by the heated earth, and the thin air of the upper levels contains far fewer molecules of gas, dust and water vapour to absorb and hold that heat. Air that rises into this thinner air also expands against the lower pressure and cools as it does so. Matches option A.
reviewNote: Rule 1: Statement 1 / Statement 2 flattened onto one line. Key A accepted on the standard textbook explanation (the troposphere is heated from below by terrestrial radiation and the thinning, less dense air aloft absorbs less of it), though strictly adiabatic expansion is the fuller cause.

It has nothing to do with a lunar mission, a disease control programme or a scheme to promote innovation. Matches option C.

subject: History
subtopic: Freedom Movement — INC, Gandhi and Independence
stem:
Arrange the following historical event/movements in chronological order:
1. Peasant movement in Bardoli
2. Resignation of Congress government ministers
3. Champaran movement
4. Peasant movements in Kheda Select the correct answer using the codes given below:
solution: Gandhi's first satyagraha on Indian soil was at Champaran in Bihar in 1917, on behalf of the indigo cultivators held to the tinkathia system. The Kheda campaign in Gujarat followed in 1918, when the peasants sought remission of revenue in a year of failed crops. Vallabhbhai Patel led the Bardoli satyagraha against an enhancement of the land revenue in 1928, and it was there that he earned the title Sardar. The Congress ministries formed under the Government of India Act of 1935 resigned in 1939, in protest at India being declared a party to the war without the Assembly being consulted. The order is therefore Champaran, Kheda, Bardoli, and the resignation of the ministries. Matches option A.
reviewNote: Rule 1: the four numbered events and the code line are flattened. Derivation: Champaran 1917 (3), Kheda 1918 (4), Bardoli 1928 (1), resignation of Congress ministries 1939 (2) = 3-4-1-2 = A.

subject: History
subtopic: Freedom Movement — INC, Gandhi and Independence
stem:
With reference to the General Elections of 1945, consider the following statements:
1. Congress won more than 90% of the Non- Muslim votes in the Central Legislative elections.
2. The Muslim League formed its ministries in NWFP and Bengal after its win in provincial elections.
Which of the statements given above is/are not correct?
solution:
Statement 1 is correct. In the elections to the Central Legislative Assembly held at the end of 1945 the Congress polled about 91 per cent of the non-Muslim votes and captured 57 of the 102 seats, while the Muslim League took all 30 of the reserved Muslim seats.

Statement 2 is not correct. After sweeping the Muslim seats in the provincial elections of early 1946 the Muslim League formed ministries in Bengal and in Sind, not in the North-West Frontier Province. In the NWFP the Congress won a clear majority and Dr Khan Sahib became Premier, which is precisely why a referendum had to be held there in 1947 before the province could go to Pakistan.

So the second statement alone is the one that is not correct. Matches option B.
reviewNote: Rule 1: statements flattened. Derivation, noting the stem asks which are NOT correct: (1) is correct - Congress took about 91 percent of the non-Muslim vote in the Central Legislative Assembly elections; (2) is NOT correct - the League formed a ministry in Bengal but NWFP went to Congress under Dr Khan Sahib. So only (2) = B.

subject: Geography
chapter: Earth's Structure, Landforms and Geological Time
stem: Which of the following statements about weathering is not correct?
optA: Weathering causes the disintegration of rocks near the surface of the earth.
optB: The minerals in rocks that are formed under high pressure and temperature are more resistant to weathering.
optC: Climate has a significance role in weathering.
optD: Weathering can occur due to chemical and mechanical processes.
solution:
Weathering is the breaking down of rock in place at or near the earth's surface, it proceeds by both mechanical and chemical means, and its rate is strongly controlled by climate, since temperature and moisture govern how fast the chemical reactions run. Those three claims are all sound.

The remaining claim reverses the real relationship. A mineral that crystallises deep inside the earth is in equilibrium with high pressure, high temperature and the absence of free oxygen and water. At the surface none of those conditions holds, so the further a mineral's conditions of formation are from surface conditions, the faster it breaks down. Olivine and pyroxene, which crystallise earliest and hottest, weather rapidly, while quartz, which crystallises last and coolest, survives to become beach sand. Minerals formed under high pressure and temperature are therefore less resistant to weathering, not more.

Matches option B.
reviewNote: Key B accepted: minerals crystallised at high pressure and temperature (top of Bowen series, e.g. olivine) are the LEAST stable at surface conditions and weather fastest, so the statement is the incorrect one.

subject: Geography
chapter: Earth's Structure, Landforms and Geological Time
subtopic: Earth's Interior, Crust and Plate Tectonics
stem: Gutenberg discontinuity is found between the :
solution:
The interior of the earth is divided by seismic discontinuities, each marking an abrupt change in the velocity of earthquake waves. The Mohorovicic discontinuity separates the crust from the mantle. The Gutenberg discontinuity lies at a depth of about 2,900 km and separates the mantle from the core; it is recognised because secondary waves, which cannot pass through a liquid, stop there, showing that the outer core is molten. The Lehmann discontinuity separates the outer core from the inner core, and the Repetti discontinuity lies between the upper and lower mantle.

Matches option B.
reviewNote: Dedup verdict was "maybe": the same Gutenberg fact appears as statement 3 of live bank row b87f4b3e-2461-48d5-8180-28a5a28e3800. Filed as new - the mock asks it as a standalone single-fact question.

subject: Geography
stem:
Arrange the following types of clouds in the increasing order of their heights:
1. Cumulus
2. Stratus
3. Cirrus
4. Nimbus
solution:
Clouds are classified partly by the height at which they form. Cirrus clouds are high clouds, thin and feathery, forming at roughly 8,000 to 12,000 m. Cumulus clouds form at middle levels, roughly 4,000 to 7,000 m, and look like heaps of cotton wool. Stratus clouds are low, layered sheets spread over large parts of the sky. Nimbus clouds are the dark grey rain clouds that form very close to the surface of the earth.

Ordered from the lowest upwards: nimbus, then stratus, then cumulus, then cirrus, that is 4, 2, 1, 3.

Matches option D.
reviewNote: Rule 1: the four numbered cloud types are flattened. Derivation using NCERT XI heights: nimbus lowest, then stratus, then cumulus (4,000-7,000 m), then cirrus (8,000-12,000 m) = 4,2,1,3 = D.

subject: Geography
chapter: Earth in Space, Maps and Coordinates
subtopic: Time Zones and International Date Line
stem: When a ship crosses the International Date Line from west to east, then its time:
solution: The International Date Line runs roughly along the meridian of one hundred and eighty degrees. Sailing eastward, a ship gains time steadily, one hour for every fifteen degrees of longitude it covers, so by the time it has crossed half the globe it is running a whole day ahead of the calendar. Crossing the line from west to east therefore requires that this whole day be given back, so the same date is lived through twice and the ship's date is set back by one full day. Matches option D.
reviewNote: [RESOLVED — a second, independent blind derivation reached the printed key (D) without seeing it or the earlier objection, so the key stands. Basis: Sailing eastward a ship gains one hour per fifteen degrees of longitude, so on reaching the 180 degree meridian it is a full day ahead of the calendar; crossing the line west to east it must give that day back, repeating the date. Concretely: leave Japan on Monday sailing east and you reach Hawaii on Sunday. So the date is set BACK one day. This is the classic reversed-key trap, since the traveller 'gains' a day in ordinary speech while the date moves backwards. D.]

subject: Geography
chapter: Earth in Space, Maps and Coordinates
subtopic: Time Zones and International Date Line
stem: Which of the following country has the maximum number of time zones?
solution:
Time zones are counted for the whole of a country's territory, including its overseas possessions. France holds territory from French Polynesia and the Marquesas in the Pacific eastward to Wallis and Futuna, and these span 12 time zones, the largest number held by any country. Russia, though the largest country by area, is one continuous land mass and spans 11. The mainland United States has four, rising to about six once Alaska and Hawaii are added, and mainland Australia has three.

Twelve is greater than eleven, so France holds the most.

Matches option B.
reviewNote: Key B accepted: counting overseas departments and territories France spans 12 time zones, ahead of Russia (11) and the USA (11).

subject: Geography
chapter: Earth's Structure, Landforms and Geological Time
stem: Which of the following is the study of the composition, texture, and structure of rocks?
solution:
Petrology takes its name from petra, meaning rock, and is exactly the branch of geology that studies rocks themselves: which minerals they are built from, how those grains are sized and arranged, which is texture, and how the rock body as a whole is put together, which is structure. Palaeontology is the study of fossils, stratigraphy is the study of the order and correlation of rock layers, and geomorphology is the study of landforms and the processes that shape them.

Matches option A.

subject: Current Affairs
stem: Which country will help the Indian Navy to co- develop UNICORN Masts?
solution:
The UNICORN, or Unified Complex Radio Antenna, is an integrated mast that houses several communication and electronic warfare antennae inside a single composite cone, so that a warship carries fewer protruding aerials and presents a smaller radar signature. The system was developed in Japan, and it is with Japan that India signed the agreement to co-develop and fit it on Indian Navy ships, making it the first completed defence equipment transfer of its kind between the two countries.

Matches option A.

subject: History
stem: The reign of Raja Krishnadev Raya is considered the golden age of which literary language?
solution:
Krishnadeva Raya of the Tuluva dynasty ruled Vijayanagara from 1509 to 1529. He was himself a Telugu poet, the author of the Amuktamalyada, and his court supported the ashtadiggajas, the eight celebrated Telugu poets led by Allasani Peddana, who is remembered as Andhra Kavita Pitamaha. His reign is for that reason described as the golden age of Telugu literature.

Matches option A.

subject: History
stem: Which one of the following is not the work of Ashvaghosha?
solution:
Ashvaghosha was a Buddhist poet and dramatist associated with the court of Kanishka in the first or second century of the Christian era. The Buddhacharita, his verse life of the Buddha, the Saundarananda, on the conversion of the Buddha's half-brother Nanda, and the drama Sariputraprakarana are all his.

The Manjushrimulakalpa is a much later anonymous Mahayana work, a Kriya Tantra text of about the sixth to eighth century, valued today mainly for the historical king-lists embedded in it. It is not his work.

Matches option D.
reviewNote: Ashvaghosha wrote Buddhacharita, Saundarananda and Sariputraprakarana; the Manjushrimulakalpa is a later Mahayana text, so D is the odd one out.

subject: History
subtopic: Freedom Movement — INC, Gandhi and Independence
stem: Who among the following took Mahatma Gandhi’s gain in the Gandhi–Irwin Pact as “Consolation Prizes”?
solution:
Under the Gandhi-Irwin Pact of March 1931 the Government agreed to release prisoners not convicted of violence, to remit unrealised fines, to return confiscated land not yet sold to third parties, and to allow people living near the coast to make salt for their own consumption. It refused the two things the Congress had pressed hardest for, an inquiry into police excesses and a commitment on the political future, and the Congress in return withdrew the Civil Disobedience Movement and agreed to attend the Second Round Table Conference.

Because the concessions dealt only with the wreckage of the movement and left the political demand untouched, Alan Campbell Johnson, who wrote the biography of Lord Halifax, the Irwin of the pact, dismissed what Gandhi had obtained as no more than consolation prizes.

Matches option B.
reviewNote: Attribution question with no internal check available (m3 prints no solutions at all). Key B accepted on the source word - Alan Campbell-Johnson, Halifax biographer, is the usual attribution for the "consolation prizes" description of Gandhi gains in the Gandhi-Irwin Pact. Worth a second eye. [blind derivation agrees with the printed key but at LOW confidence: Low confidence: this is an attribution of a quoted phrase rather than something derivable from the question. The reasoning that the concessions were peripheral is solid, but which writer coined 'consolation prizes' has to be checked against the source text. S.C. Bose is a plausible alternative, since he attacked the pact as having gained nothing substantial. Route to a human.]

subject: History
stem: In between which of the rivers was the territory of Porus, who offered strong resistance to Alexander, situated?
solution:
Porus, the Paurava king, ruled the tract lying between the Jhelum, which the Greeks called the Hydaspes, and the Chenab, which they called the Acesines. Alexander crossed the Jhelum in 326 BC and fought him on its far bank in what the Greek writers call the Battle of the Hydaspes; after the defeat Alexander restored the kingdom to Porus and added territory to it. The tract between the Ravi and the Beas belonged to the Kathaioi and other tribes, and the Ganga-Yamuna doab lay far outside Alexander's advance.

Matches option B.

subject: History
stem: Where was the ‘Battle of ten Kings’ fought?
solution:
The Dasarajna, the Battle of the Ten Kings, is described in the seventh mandala of the Rigveda. Sudas, king of the Bharatas, was attacked by a confederacy of ten tribes and defeated them on the bank of the Parushni, which is the river now called the Ravi. The Vedic names of the other rivers offered are Asikni for the Chenab, Vitasta for the Jhelum and Vipas for the Beas, so none of those is the site of the battle.

Matches option B.

subject: History
stem:
Which of the following items and the place of their discovery is wrongly matched?
1. Statuette of a bearded man – Mohenjodaro
2. Rice husks – Lothal
3. Fire pits and altars – Harappa
4. Bead-makers shop – Chanhudaro
5. Fossil remains of a horse –Surkotda
solution:
Take the pairs one at a time. The small steatite bust of a bearded man, often called the priest-king, comes from Mohenjodaro. Rice husks embedded in pottery were recovered at Lothal in Gujarat, along with Rangpur the only Harappan sites to yield them. A bead-makers' workshop, complete with furnaces, drills and unfinished beads, was found at Chanhudaro. Bones identified as those of a horse were reported from Surkotada.

The remaining pair is the mismatch. The rows of fire pits and fire altars are the distinguishing feature of Kalibangan, where they were found both on the citadel and in houses of the lower town, with further examples at Lothal and Banawali. They are not a find from Harappa.

So the third pair is wrongly matched. Matches option A.
reviewNote: Rule 2 (shape): a five-row item-and-site pair list flattened into prose rather than a GFM pipe table. Derivation: fire pits and altars are the signature of KALIBANGAN (also Lothal and Banawali), not Harappa, so item 3 is the wrongly matched pair = A; the other four pairs are correct. Sibling-confirmed by live bank row 26bbfc44, which keys Kalibangan for fire altars.

subject: History
stem: What are Nivi, Paridhan and Adhivasa?
optA: Different types of garments of the Aryans.
optB: Government officials of the Aryan kings.
solution:
These are Vedic words for clothing. The nivi is the lower garment wrapped about the waist, the paridhana, also called vasas, is the main garment worn over it, and the adhivasa is the outer wrap or mantle. Taken together they name the three layers of dress described in the Vedic texts, so they are garments and not officials, tribes or musical instruments.

Matches option A.

subject: Economics
stem:
Which of the following is/are correct statements regarding the ‘Washington Consensus’?
1. The consensus in Washington about matters of foreign policy.
2. The ten–point guideline to liberal economic reform for development around the world.
3. The ten–point guideline for economic growth in Europe.
Select the correct answer from the codes given below:
solution:
The Washington Consensus is the name John Williamson gave in 1989 to a set of ten policy prescriptions on which the International Monetary Fund, the World Bank and the United States Treasury, all headquartered in Washington, had converged. The ten points include fiscal discipline, redirection of public spending, tax reform, liberalised interest rates and trade, a competitive exchange rate, openness to foreign direct investment, privatisation, deregulation and secure property rights.

Statement 1 is not correct: the term has nothing to do with foreign policy, it is a package of economic prescriptions.
Statement 2 is correct: it is precisely a ten-point guideline for liberal economic reform, urged on countries around the world as the path to development.
Statement 3 is not correct: it was addressed to developing economies, Latin America above all, and not to Europe.

Only the second statement is correct. Matches option B.
reviewNote: Rule 1: statements flattened. Derivation: the Washington Consensus is the John Williamson 1989 ten-point liberal-reform prescription for developing economies, so only (2); (3) mislocates it in Europe. Filing is a compromise - the Economics subject has only the "Indian Economy" chapter and this is world economics.

subject: History
stem:
Consider the following statements with respect to the Jacobin Club.
1. Its members largely came from the less prosperous sections of society.
2. Robespierre was the leader of Jacobin Club.
3. ‘Sans-culottes’ was a rival group of the Jacobin Club.
Which of the above is / are correct?
solution:
Statement 1 is correct. The members of the Jacobin club came mainly from the less prosperous sections of society: small shopkeepers and artisans such as shoemakers, pastry cooks, watchmakers and printers, together with servants and daily-wage workers.

Statement 2 is correct. The club was led by Maximilian Robespierre, who went on to dominate the period of the Terror.

Statement 3 is not correct. Sans-culottes was not a rival group at all. It was the name the Jacobins themselves adopted, meaning those without knee breeches, because they wore the long striped trousers of dock workers in place of the knee breeches worn by the nobility.

So the first two statements are correct and the third is not. Matches option D.
reviewNote: Rule 1: statements flattened. Derivation: (1) and (2) are true; (3) is false - "sans-culottes" was the name the Jacobins themselves went by, not a rival group. So (1) and (2) = D.

subject: Polity
chapter: World Polity, Democracy and International Relations
stem: Who gave the concept of ‘Separation of Powers’ related to different forms of governments?
solution:
Montesquieu set out the doctrine in The Spirit of the Laws in 1748. His argument was that the legislative, executive and judicial powers of a state must be lodged in different hands, because when the same body frames a law, enforces it and then judges disputes arising under it, nothing checks its power. Aristotle had classified forms of government and had noticed three elements within the state, but he did not propose separating the three powers as a safeguard against tyranny. Plato described an ideal state ruled by philosopher-kings, and Hobbes argued that sovereign power must be undivided, which is the opposite proposition.

Matches option A.

subject: History
stem: With reference to the Mughal Empire, the term ‘harem’ pertains to:
optA: The initiative of building marble monuments.
optB: The Deccan Policy of the Mughals.
solution:
Harem comes from the Persian haram, meaning a sacred or forbidden place. In writing about the Mughals the word stands for the imperial household itself: the emperor's wives and concubines, his mother, sisters and other female relatives, and the servants, slaves and eunuchs who attended them. Historians use it as the entry into the domestic world of the Mughals, and the chief source for it is Gulbadan Begum's Humayun Nama, written by a woman of the household. It has nothing to do with Mughal building, with the Deccan campaigns or with revenue.

Matches option D.

subject: Geography
stem:
Consider the following statements regarding migration.
1. Net migration is the total change in the number of in-migrants and outmigrants.
2. As per the 2011 census, Delhi and Mumbai are migrant magnets.
3. Higher employment opportunities are one of the push factors of migration.
How many of the above statements is/are correct?
solution:
Statement 1 is correct. People arriving at a place are in-migrants and people leaving it are out-migrants; net migration is the change that the two together produce in the population, that is, in-migrants less out-migrants. Where it is positive the place is gaining people, where negative it is losing them.

Statement 2 is correct. The 2011 census shows internal migration streams converging on a few destinations, of which Greater Mumbai and Delhi are much the largest, so both function as magnets for migrants.

Statement 3 is not correct. Better employment prospects exist at the destination and draw people towards it, so higher employment opportunity is a pull factor. Push factors operate at the place of origin and are things such as unemployment, poverty, drought, flood and social discrimination.

Two of the three statements are correct. Matches option B.
reviewNote: Rule 1: statements flattened. Derivation: (3) is false - employment opportunity is a PULL factor, not a push factor; (2) is true; (1) is loosely worded ("total change" for the difference between in- and out-migrants) but is read as true, giving 2 correct = B. If (1) were judged wrong the answer would be A, so this one is worth a second eye.

subject: Geography
stem:
Consider the following statements regarding the spring tides:
1. During spring tide, the sun, the moon and the earth are in a straight line.
2. The height of the tide will be higher during spring tide.
3. Spring tides occur once a month. How many of the above statements is/are correct?
solution:
Statement 1 is correct. A spring tide occurs when the sun, the moon and the earth lie in a straight line, which happens at new moon, with sun and moon on the same side of the earth, and at full moon, with them on opposite sides.

Statement 2 is correct. In that alignment the tide-raising pull of the sun reinforces that of the moon instead of working across it, so the combined force is at its greatest and the high tides run unusually high while the low tides fall unusually low.

Statement 3 is not correct. Because the alignment is reached at both new moon and full moon, spring tides occur twice in a lunar month, about a fortnight apart, and not once.

Two of the three statements are correct. Matches option B.
reviewNote: Rule 1: statements flattened. Derivation: (1) and (2) true; (3) false - spring tides occur TWICE a month, at new moon and full moon. Two correct = B.

subject: Geography
chapter: Earth's Structure, Landforms and Geological Time
subtopic: Earth's Interior, Crust and Plate Tectonics
stem:
Examine these two statements carefully and select the answer using the code given below.
Statement I: The oceanic crust mainly consists of silica and magnesium.
Statement II: It is therefore called SIMA.
optA: Both the statements are individually true and Statement II is the correct explanation of Statement I.
optB: Both the statement are individually true but Statement II is not the correct explanation of Statement I.
optC: Statement I is true but Statement II is false.
optD: Statement I is false but Statement II is true.
solution:
The continental crust is built largely of silica and aluminium and is called SIAL, a name made from the first syllables of those two words. The oceanic crust is basaltic, richer in magnesium and poorer in aluminium, and is named SIMA on exactly the same principle, from silica and magnesium.

The first statement is therefore true, the second statement is true, and the second is the correct explanation of the first: the name SIMA is built out of the very composition the first statement describes, so the composition is the reason for the name.

Matches option A.
reviewNote: Rule 1: Statement I / Statement II flattened onto one line.

subject: Polity
chapter: Government Structure — Parliament, Judiciary and Constitutional Bodies
stem: In India, which of the following has the power to negotiate foreign treaties?
solution:
Negotiating and concluding a treaty is an executive act. The executive power of the Union is vested in the President by Article 53, and Article 73 extends that power to every matter on which Parliament may legislate, which by Entry 14 of the Union List includes entering into treaties and agreements with foreign countries. Treaties are accordingly negotiated and signed in the name of the President.

Parliament's role is a different one: under Article 253 it makes the laws needed to give a treaty effect inside India. The Prime Minister works through the Council of Ministers, which aids and advises the President and does not itself hold the treaty-making power, and the Speaker presides over the Lok Sabha and has no function in external affairs at all.

Matches option B.

subject: History
stem: Who among the following was a contributor to the subject of medicine in ancient India?
solution:
Charaka, physician at the court of Kanishka, compiled the Charaka Samhita, the foundational text of Indian medicine, which deals with diagnosis, diet, ethics and treatment and remained in use for centuries. Of the others, Bhasa was a Sanskrit dramatist, remembered for the Svapnavasavadatta, Panini was the grammarian who composed the Ashtadhyayi, and Harsha was a seventh century king who was himself the author of plays such as Ratnavali.

Matches option B.

subject: Geography

stem:
Consider the following statements regarding the Golden Quadrilateral super highways.
1. These highway projects are being implemented by the Border Road Organisation.
2. It forms a quadrilateral connecting the four major metro cities of India. Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
solution:
Statement 1 is not correct. The Golden Quadrilateral, together with the North-South and East-West corridors, forms part of the National Highways Development Project and is executed by the National Highways Authority of India. The Border Roads Organisation has an entirely different charge, building and maintaining roads in the strategically sensitive border areas of the north and north-east.

Statement 2 is correct. The Golden Quadrilateral is a six-lane highway of about 5,846 km joining Delhi, Kolkata, Chennai and Mumbai, and the four legs enclose a quadrilateral, which is where the name comes from.

Only the second statement is correct. Matches option B.

subject: Geography
chapter: Indian Geography — Economy, Resources and Transport
stem: Which of the following economic activities are directly dependent on environment?
solution:
Primary activities are those in which people take a product straight out of nature: gathering, hunting, fishing, forestry, mining and agriculture. Whether such an activity is possible at all, and how much it yields, is settled by soil, climate, relief and the presence of ore, timber or fish, so these activities depend on the environment directly.

Secondary activities process what the primary sector has already extracted, so nature reaches them only at one remove. Tertiary activities supply services such as transport, trade and banking, and quaternary activities deal in knowledge, research and information, and both stand further away still.

Matches option A.

subject: Geography
subtopic: Indian Rivers, Lakes and Water Bodies
stem:
Consider the following statements in light of the drainage system in India.
1. Most of the Himalayan rivers are perennial.
2. Himalayan rivers are dependent on South-west monsoon rainfall for their water.
3. Peninsular rivers receive water from only melted snow from the lofty mountains.
How many of the statements given above is/are correct?
solution:
Statement 1 is correct. The Himalayan rivers rise in or beyond the high Himalayas and are fed by the melting of snow and glaciers as well as by rain, so they carry water throughout the year and are perennial.

Statement 2 is not correct. Dependence on the south-west monsoon rains for their supply is the mark of the Peninsular rivers, which is exactly why most of them shrink to a trickle in the dry season. It is the meltwater supply, not the monsoon, that keeps the Himalayan rivers flowing when the rains have gone; to call them dependent on monsoon rainfall would contradict their perennial character described in the first statement.

Statement 3 is not correct, and it reverses the same fact. The Peninsular rivers rise in low hills such as the Western Ghats and the Amarkantak plateau, where no permanent snow lies, so they receive no meltwater whatever and depend entirely on rainfall.

Only the first statement is correct. Matches option A.
reviewNote: Rule 1: statements flattened. Derivation: (1) true; (3) false - peninsular rivers are rain-fed and have no snow source at all; (2) is treated as false because Himalayan rivers are perennial precisely BECAUSE they draw on snowmelt as well as monsoon rain, so "dependent on South-west monsoon rainfall for their water" misstates it. One correct = A, agreeing with the key. Statement (2) is genuinely loosely worded and is the one to re-read if this is ever disputed.

subject: Current Affairs
subtopic: Indian Navy — Ships, Vessels and Naval Policy
stem: Which of the following is India’s second nuclear- powered submarine?
solution:
India's first indigenous nuclear-powered ballistic missile submarine was INS Arihant, commissioned in 2016. The second boat of the same class, INS Arighaat, was commissioned at Visakhapatnam in August 2024, making it India's second nuclear-powered submarine. INS Aridhaman is the third boat of the class and is yet to be commissioned, and INS Viraat was a conventionally powered aircraft carrier, now decommissioned, and not a submarine at all.

Matches option B.

subject: Current Affairs

solution:
Joe Biden was the 46th President of the United States and held office from 2021 to 2025. Donald Trump, who had already served as the 45th President from 2017 to 2021, won the election of November 2024 and was sworn in on 20 January 2025 as the 47th President. Because his two terms are not consecutive he is counted twice in the numbering, in the same way that Grover Cleveland is counted as the 22nd and 24th President. Kamala Harris was Vice President and the defeated candidate in that election.

Matches option A.

solution: The question asks for the pair that is wrongly matched, so three of the four pairings will hold and one will fail. subject: Chemistry
stem: What is iodised table salt?
solution: Ordinary table salt is sodium chloride, but iodised salt has a small quantity of a potassium iodide or iodate added to it, so more than one substance is present and it can be neither an element nor a single compound. The added iodine compound is spread uniformly through the salt, so every sample taken from it has the same composition and no separate parts can be picked out even under a microscope. Any mixture whose composition is uniform throughout is called a homogeneous mixture. Matches option D.

This is publisher practice material rather than a past paper, so there is no issued key to preserve. The book prints C. Basis: Iodised salt is sodium chloride with a small quantity of potassium iodide or potassium iodate added, so it contains more than one substance and cannot be an element or a single compound. The added iodine compound is distributed uniformly, so the composition is the same throughout and no boundary between components is visible, which makes it homogeneous, not heterogeneous. D.]

subject: Biology
stem: In human body, which one of the following one of the following serves as the blood bank of the human body?
solution:
The spleen holds a reserve of blood in its sinusoids and discharges it into circulation when the body needs it, as after a haemorrhage or during heavy exertion, and for that reason it is called the blood bank of the body. It also filters the blood and destroys worn-out red cells. Of the other organs, the liver stores glycogen, iron and fat-soluble vitamins, the pancreas secretes digestive enzymes and the hormones insulin and glucagon, and the lymph nodes filter lymph and produce lymphocytes.

Matches option C.

subject: Chemistry
subtopic: Common Acids: Names, Formulas and Uses
stem: Which one of the following acids is used for etching glass?
solution:
Glass is chiefly silicon dioxide, and it resists sulphuric, nitric and hydrochloric acid, which is why those acids can be kept in glass bottles in the laboratory at all. Hydrofluoric acid is the exception. It attacks silica, converting it to silicon tetrafluoride and water, so it bites into the glass surface wherever the glass is not protected by a wax coating. That reaction is what is used to etch markings and designs onto glassware, and it is also the reason hydrofluoric acid itself must be stored in plastic or wax-lined containers.

Matches option C.

subject: Physics
stem: Spot the wrong statement. The acceleration due to gravity ‘g’ decreases if
optA: We go down from the surface of the earth towards its centre.
optB: We go up from the surface of the earth.
optC: We go from the equator towards the poles on the surface of the earth.
optD: The rotational velocity of the earth is increased.
solution: The question asks which statement is wrong, so the answer is the case in which the acceleration due to gravity does not in fact decrease. Below the surface the value of g falls off in proportion to the distance from the centre, so going down does reduce it. Above the surface g falls off as the inverse square of the distance from the centre, so going up reduces it as well. Increasing the rate of the earth's rotation increases the centrifugal effect that opposes gravity, so the effective value of g falls there too. Moving from the equator towards the poles, however, both effects work the other way: the earth's radius is smaller at the poles and the centrifugal effect vanishes there, so g is greatest at the poles. Saying that g decreases as we go from the equator to the poles is therefore the wrong statement. Matches option C.
reviewNote: [RESOLVED — a second, independent blind derivation reached the printed key (C) without seeing it or the earlier objection, so the key stands. Basis: Polarity stated first: 'Spot the wrong statement' means find the case in which g does NOT decrease. Going down, g falls as g(1 - d/R): decrease, so A is a true statement. Going up, g falls as inverse square: decrease, so B is true. Increasing the earth's angular speed increases the centrifugal term in g_eff = g - (omega squared)R cos-squared(latitude): decrease, so D is true. From equator to pole g INCREASES, because the radius is smaller and the centrifugal term vanishes, so the claim that g decreases there is the wrong statement. C.]

subject: Physics
stem: Magnetic, electrostatic and gravitational forces are which type of forces?
solution:
Contact forces act only while two bodies are touching, as friction and the normal reaction do. Magnetic force acts between a magnet and a piece of iron across an air gap, electrostatic force acts between two charged bodies across a gap, and gravitational force holds the moon in its orbit across a quarter of a million miles of empty space. None of the three requires the bodies to touch: each source sets up a field around itself and the force is exerted through that field. All three are therefore non-contact forces.

Matches option A.

subject: Chemistry
stem: Consider the following statements. (i) On strong heating, washing gives sodium oxide and carbon dioxide. (ii) Plaster of Paris is obtained by heating gypsum at 373K. (iii) Bleaching powder is used for disinfecting drinking water. Which of these statement(s) is/ are correct?
solution:
Take the three statements one at a time.

The first is correct. Washing soda is sodium carbonate. Strong heating breaks the carbonate down into the oxide and carbon dioxide, \(\mathrm{Na_2CO_3 \rightarrow Na_2O + CO_2}\).

The second is correct. Gypsum is calcium sulphate dihydrate, \(\mathrm{CaSO_4 \cdot 2H_2O}\). Heated to 373 K it loses three quarters of its water and becomes calcium sulphate hemihydrate, \(\mathrm{CaSO_4 \cdot \tfrac{1}{2}H_2O}\), which is plaster of Paris. The temperature matters: heated much above this it loses the remaining water and the product will no longer set.

The third is correct. Bleaching powder, calcium oxychloride, releases chlorine on contact with water and is used to disinfect drinking water and swimming pools as well as to bleach cloth and wood pulp.

All three statements are correct. Matches option D.
reviewNote: Rule 1: the three roman-numbered statements are flattened into one line. TEXT DEFECT, not answer-affecting: statement (i) reads "On strong heating, washing gives sodium oxide and carbon dioxide" - the word "soda" has been dropped and it must read "washing soda" (Na2CO3 gives Na2O + CO2). Derivation: all three statements are true, so D. Repair the dropped word before publishing.

subject: Chemistry
stem: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
solution:
Check each pair. Horn silver, the mineral cerargyrite, is silver chloride and not silver iodide. Artificial rain is produced by seeding clouds with silver iodide, whose crystal lattice resembles that of ice and so gives supercooled droplets something to freeze onto, and not with silver chloride; the first two pairs have simply had their silver salts interchanged. Philosopher's wool is the old name for zinc oxide, from the woolly white deposit that forms when zinc is burnt in air, not zinc sulphide.

The remaining pair is sound. Zinc phosphide is genuinely used as a rodenticide: in the animal's stomach it reacts with the acid there and releases phosphine, which is the poison.

Matches option C.
reviewNote: Derivation: horn silver is AgCl not AgI; artificial rain uses AgI not AgCl; philosopher wool is ZnO not ZnS; only zinc phosphide = rat poison is correct, so C. NOTE: this stem is character-identical to Q126 ("Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?") but the two questions are DIFFERENT - the option sets share nothing. Not an internal duplicate.

subject: Physics
subtopic: Refraction, Speed of Light and TIR
stem: Total internal reflection is possible when light rays travel:
solution:
Total internal reflection can happen only when light passes from an optically denser medium into a rarer one, because only then does the refracted ray bend away from the normal, so that at a large enough angle of incidence it grazes the boundary and beyond that angle cannot emerge at all.

Compare the refractive indices: air about 1.00, water about 1.33, glass about 1.50. Air to water, air to glass and water to glass all pass from the rarer medium to the denser one, where the ray bends towards the normal and no critical angle exists. Only glass to water passes from denser to rarer, and there the critical angle is \(\sin^{-1}(1.33/1.50)\), about 62 degrees.

Matches option C.

subject: Physics
stem: Two bodies A and B having masses m and 4 m respectively are moving with equal linear momentum. The ratio of kinetic energies between A and B is:
solution:
Rewrite kinetic energy in terms of momentum. From \(p = mv\) we have \(v = p/m\), so \(KE = \tfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = \tfrac{1}{2}m(p/m)^2 = p^2/(2m)\). At a fixed momentum, therefore, kinetic energy is inversely proportional to mass: the heavier body carries the smaller share.

The lighter body has mass \(m\) and the heavier has mass \(4m\), and the two carry equal momentum \(p\). Their kinetic energies are \(p^2/(2m)\) and \(p^2/(8m)\), so the ratio is \(\dfrac{p^2/(2m)}{p^2/(8m)} = \dfrac{8m}{2m} = 4\).

Taken in the order asked, lighter body first, the ratio is 4 to 1. Matches option B.
reviewNote: Derivation: KE = p^2/2m at equal p, so KE_A : KE_B = (1/m) : (1/4m) = 4 : 1 = B.

subject: Physics
stem: Which one of the following is not correctly matched?
solution:
Check each instrument against the quantity written beside it. The voltmeter is connected across a component and reads the potential difference between its ends. The galvanometer detects and measures small electric currents. The metre bridge is the practical form of the Wheatstone bridge and is used to find an unknown resistance.

The potentiometer, however, does not measure charge. It compares potential differences by balancing the unknown against the fall of potential along a uniform current-carrying wire, and is used chiefly to measure the emf of a cell and the internal resistance of a cell. Its particular virtue is that at balance it draws no current from the cell under test. Charge is measured by a ballistic galvanometer or an electrometer, so that is the pair which does not match.

Matches option B.

subject: Physics
stem:
Match List I with List II and select the correct answer from the codes given below:

| List I (Position of objects) | List II (Magnification) |
|---|---|
| (I) An object is placed at focus before a convex mirror | (A) Magnification is \(-\infty\) |
| (II) An object is placed at centre of curvature before a concave mirror | (B) Magnification is 0.5 |
| (III) An object is placed at focus before a concave mirror | (C) Magnification is +1 |
| (IV) An object is placed at centre of curvature before a convex mirror | (D) Magnification is \(-1\) |
| | (E) Magnification is 0.33 |
solution:
Work with numerical focal length \(f\) and object distance \(d\), both positive lengths, and recall that the centre of curvature lies at \(d = 2f\). For a convex mirror the magnification is \(m = f/(d+f)\), and for a concave mirror it is \(m = f/(f-d)\).

Object at the focus of a convex mirror: \(m = f/(f+f) = 1/2\), a magnification of 0.5, the image being erect and diminished.

Object at the centre of curvature of a concave mirror: \(m = f/(f-2f) = -1\). The image is real, inverted and the same size as the object, formed at the centre of curvature itself.

Object at the focus of a concave mirror: \(m = f/(f-f)\), where the denominator vanishes. The reflected rays leave parallel, the image is thrown to infinity and the magnification is unbounded, written \(-\infty\) because the image is inverted.

Object at the centre of curvature of a convex mirror: \(m = f/(2f+f) = 1/3\), a magnification of about 0.33.

The four positions therefore give 0.5, then \(-1\), then \(-\infty\), then 0.33. Matches option A.
reviewNote: Rule 2: a two-column match list (I-IV against A-E) flattened into prose. Derivation, all four verified: (I) object at f before a CONVEX mirror gives v = f/2 and m = +0.5, so B; (II) object at C before a CONCAVE mirror gives m = -1, so D; (III) object at f before a CONCAVE mirror sends the image to infinity, m = -infinity, so A; (IV) object at C before a CONVEX mirror gives v = 2f/3 and m = +1/3 = 0.33, so E. That is I-B, II-D, III-A, IV-E = option A, matching the key.

Tuberculosis is screened for by the Mantoux test, in which tuberculin is injected into the skin of the forearm and the size of the induration read after 48 to 72 hours, so that pair takes item 4. subject: Physics
stem: On which of the given parameters specific resistance depends?
solution:
The resistance of a wire depends on its dimensions through \(R = \rho l/A\), but the specific resistance \(\rho\) appearing in that formula is a property of the material itself, defined as the resistance of a specimen of unit length and unit cross-sectional area. Because length and area have already been divided out in the definition, \(\rho\) does not change when the same wire is drawn longer or thicker, and it does not depend on the current, since Ohm's law holds at constant temperature and \(\rho\) is what makes it hold.

What does alter it, besides the choice of material, is temperature. In a metal \(\rho\) rises as the temperature rises, because the lattice vibrates more strongly and scatters the drifting electrons more often; in a semiconductor it falls, because heating frees more charge carriers.

Matches option D.
reviewNote: Resistivity is a material property - independent of length, cross-section and current, but temperature-dependent. D.

subject: Physics
stem:
Consider the following statements.
Statement I: When a gun is fired it recoils i.e. it pushes back, with much less velocity than the velocity of the bullet.
Statement II: Velocity of the recoiling gun is less because the gun is much heavier than the bullet.
optA: Both the statement are correct and statement II is the correct explanation of statement I.
optB: Both the statements are correct, but statement II is not the correct explanation of statement I.
optC: Statement I is correct but statement II is incorrect.
optD: Statement I is incorrect but statement II is correct.
solution:
Before the shot the gun and the bullet are both at rest, so the total momentum of the system is zero, and while the powder burns the forces between gun and bullet are internal, with no external horizontal force acting. Momentum is therefore conserved, and the momentum of the gun backwards must equal that of the bullet forwards: \(m_g v_g = m_b v_b\).

Rearranging gives \(v_g = (m_b/m_g)\,v_b\). The gun is many times heavier than the bullet, so the fraction \(m_b/m_g\) is very small and the recoil speed is a correspondingly small fraction of the bullet's speed.

Both statements are true, and the second is precisely the reason for the first: it is the large mass of the gun standing in the denominator that makes the recoil velocity small.

Matches option A.
reviewNote: Rule 1: Statement I / Statement II flattened onto one line.

subject: Biology
stem: Which of the following is incorrectly matched?
solution:
Check each pair. The neuron is the structural and functional unit of the nervous system. The nephron is the structural and functional unit of the kidney. Thrombocytes, the platelets, are formed elements of the blood and belong with the circulatory system, where they seal injured vessels and start the clotting cascade.

Erythrocytes, the red blood cells, also belong to the circulatory system and not to the lymphatic system. Lymph is blood plasma that has escaped from the capillaries into the tissue spaces and then drained into lymph vessels; it carries lymphocytes but contains no red blood cells at all, which is why it is colourless rather than red. That pair is therefore the incorrect one.

Matches option D.

subject: Physics
stem: If a charged particle moves through a magnetic field perpendicular to it:
optA: both momentum and energy of particle change.
optB: momentum as well as energy are constant.
optC: energy is constant but momentum changes.
optD: momentum is constant but energy changes.
solution: The magnetic force on a moving charge is \(\vec{F} = q(\vec{v} \times \vec{B})\). A cross product is perpendicular to both of the vectors that form it, so \(\vec{F}\) is always perpendicular to \(\vec{v}\). The rate at which the force does work is \(\vec{F} \cdot \vec{v}\), and this is zero because the two are at right angles. A force that does no work cannot change the kinetic energy, so the speed and the energy of the particle stay exactly what they were. The force itself is not zero, however. It keeps pulling the particle sideways and bends the path into a circle, so the direction of the velocity is changing all the time. Momentum \(\vec{p} = m\vec{v}\) is a vector quantity, and a change of direction alone is already a change in it, even though its magnitude never alters. Hence the energy is constant while the momentum changes. Matches option C.
reviewNote: The magnetic force is always perpendicular to v, so it does no work: speed and kinetic energy are constant while the momentum VECTOR changes direction. C.

subject: Biology
stem: Which one of the following is considered as a cell within a cell?
solution: A chloroplast is bounded by a double membrane and carries its own circular DNA, its own 70S ribosomes and its own machinery for making proteins, and it multiplies by dividing inside the host cell rather than being built afresh each time. Because it can partly run and reproduce itself in this way it is called semi-autonomous, and is described as a cell within a cell. The other three organelles cannot do any of this: a ribosome is only a particle of RNA and protein with no membrane at all, a lysosome is a single-membrane sac of digestive enzymes, and the Golgi complex is a stack of flattened cisternae. None of them carries DNA or divides on its own. Matches option B.

subject: Biology
stem: Which of the following statements is correct?
optA: A seed is a ripened ovary.
optB: A seed is a ripened flower.
optC: A seed is a ripened gynoecium.
optD: A seed is a ripened ovule.
solution: After fertilisation each part of the flower has a definite fate. The ovule, which contains the fertilised egg, develops into the seed, while the ovary that enclosed the ovules ripens into the fruit around it. So a seed is a ripened ovule and a fruit is a ripened ovary, which rules out the first statement. The gynoecium is the whole female part of the flower, made of ovary, style and stigma, so it is far larger than a seed, and the flower as a whole withers away once fertilisation is over. Matches option D.

subject: Biology
stem: Which one of the following causes the disease Syphilis?
solution: Syphilis is a sexually transmitted disease caused by Treponema pallidum, a spirally coiled bacterium belonging to the group called spirochaetes. Because the organism is a bacterium it can be killed by antibiotics, and penicillin remains the standard treatment. This is what separates it from a viral sexually transmitted infection such as AIDS, which antibiotics cannot touch. Matches option A.

subject: Biology
stem: Who among the following was the first person to observe bacteria through microscope?
solution: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek ground his own single-lens microscopes and in 1676 became the first person to see and describe living bacteria, which he called animalcules, in samples of water, saliva and scrapings from his own teeth. Robert Hooke had earlier examined a thin slice of cork and coined the word cell, but what he saw were the empty walls of dead plant cells, not bacteria. Louis Pasteur later showed that microbes cause fermentation and disease, and Rudolf Virchow stated that every cell arises from a pre-existing cell; both of these came long after bacteria had first been observed. Matches option A.

stem: Which one of the following is NOT correct?
optA: Theory of evolution was propounded by Charles Darwin.
optB: The breaking of the nucleus of an atom is called fusion.
optC: Dry ice is nothing but solid carbon dioxide.
optD: Telephone was invented by Graham Bell.
solution: Test each statement in turn. The theory of evolution by natural selection was indeed put forward by Charles Darwin. Dry ice is indeed solid carbon dioxide, which turns straight into gas without melting. The telephone was indeed invented by Alexander Graham Bell. The one remaining statement is the false one: the breaking up of a heavy nucleus into lighter fragments is called fission, and it is the joining together of light nuclei into a heavier one that is called fusion. The statement has these two names interchanged, so it is the statement that is not correct. Matches option B.

subject: Physics
stem: Which one of the following pairs is correctly matched?
optD: Measurement of charge of an electron : Aston
solution: Check each pair against the scientist who actually did the work. Moseley measured the X-ray spectra of the elements and showed that the frequency of the characteristic lines depends on the nuclear charge; this established atomic number, rather than atomic mass, as the true basis of the periodic table, so that pairing is correct. Of the rest, the mass spectrograph was built by Aston, not Chadwick; the neutron was discovered by Chadwick, not Millikan; and the charge on the electron was measured by Millikan in his oil-drop experiment, not by Aston. The three wrong pairs are these same three names shuffled among one another. Matches option B.

subject: Physics
stem: The image formed by convex mirror of a real object is larger the object:
solution: For a convex mirror the centre of curvature and the focus both lie behind the reflecting surface, so rays from a real object always diverge after reflection and only appear to come from a point behind the mirror. The image is therefore virtual and erect for every position of the object, and it is always formed between the pole and the focus. Since the whole image, however large the object, has to fit into that short strip behind the mirror, the magnification is less than one whatever the object distance may be. The image can never equal or exceed the size of the object, so there is no value of u for which it is larger. This shrinking is exactly why convex mirrors are used as rear-view and blind-corner mirrors: a diminished image means a wide field of view. Matches option D.
reviewNote: A convex mirror forms a virtual, erect, diminished image of a real object for every object distance, so the image is never larger - D.

subject: Physics
subtopic: Magnetism and Magnetic Effects of Current
stem: A current carrying power line carries current from west to east. Then the direction of the magnetic field 2 m above it is:
solution: Take the three directions east, north and vertically upwards. By the Biot-Savart rule the magnetic field of a straight wire points along the direction of the current crossed with the direction that runs from the wire to the point in question. Here the current runs towards the east and the point lies straight up from the wire, and east crossed with up gives south. The right-hand grip rule gives the same thing: hold the wire in the right hand with the thumb pointing east along the current, and the curled fingers show the field circling the wire, passing from north towards south as they sweep over the top of it. So at a point 2 m above the power line the field is directed from north to south. Matches option C.
reviewNote: Derivation with x = east, y = north, z = up: B is along I_hat cross r_hat = x_hat cross z_hat = -y_hat, i.e. pointing south, so above the conductor the field runs north to south = C.

subject: Physics
stem: Which one among the following statements is correct?
optA: Convex mirrors are used by doctors to examine oral cavity.
optB: Concave mirrors are used as reflectors.
optC: Convex mirrors are used as reflectors.
optD: Convex mirrors should be used for shaving.
solution: Doctors and dentists need an enlarged upright image of a small cavity, and only a concave mirror gives that, when the object lies within its focus, so a convex mirror will not serve for examining the oral cavity. For the same reason a shaving mirror must be concave, since a convex mirror always forms a diminished image. The reflector in a torch, a headlight or a searchlight has to gather the light of a source placed at the focus and send it out as a parallel beam, and that is precisely what a concave mirror does, whereas a convex mirror would spread the light out. The only correct statement is therefore that concave mirrors are used as reflectors. Matches option B.

Basis: A: dentists need a magnified erect image of a small cavity, which only a concave mirror gives (object inside focus), so A is false. D: shaving mirrors are concave for the same reason; a convex mirror always gives a diminished image, so D is false. C: a reflector must collect light from a source at the focus and send out a parallel beam, which a concave mirror does; a convex mirror diverges the beam, so C is false. B is the only true statement.]

stem: According to Ampere’s Circuital law
solution: Ampere's circuital law is a statement about the CLOSED line integral of the magnetic field taken round a loop, so the correct expression must use a closed integral, must pair the field with a length element, and must combine them with a dot product, since it is the component of the field ALONG the path that contributes. Only one expression does all three: the closed integral of the field dotted with \(dl\). Its right-hand side must also be non-zero and must carry the current enclosed, because a loop enclosing a current has non-zero circulation; the constant of proportionality is the permeability of free space, giving \(\mu_{0} I\). The two expressions built on a cross product fail on the operator and equate the circulation to zero, which is false for any loop enclosing a current, and one of them integrates \(dt\) rather than a length element. The remaining expression also integrates \(dt\) and attaches a factor \(4\pi\), which belongs to the Biot-Savart constant \(\mu_{0}/4\pi\) and not to the circuital law. Matches option B.

subject: Chemistry
stem: Alum is used as
solution: Alum dissolves to give \(\mathrm{Al}^{3+}\) ions, which react with water to throw down a sticky, jelly-like precipitate of aluminium hydroxide. This floc is positively charged, so it neutralises the negatively charged particles of clay and silt that keep muddy water permanently suspended; the particles then stick together into larger lumps and settle to the bottom. Alum is therefore used as a coagulant to clarify drinking water. It has no pain-relieving action, it adds no nitrogen or phosphorus to the soil so it is not a fertiliser, and it does not kill germs, which is why the clarified water must still be chlorinated separately. Matches option D.

subject: Physics
stem: Two sphere of mass m and M are situated in air and the gravitational force between them is F. The space around the masses is now filled with a liquid of specific gravity 3. The gravitational forces will now be:
solution: Newton's law of gravitation gives the force between two masses as \(F = GmM/r^{2}\). The only quantities entering it are the two masses, the distance between them and the universal constant \(G\); nothing in the expression refers to what fills the space between the bodies. Gravitation, unlike the electrostatic force between charges, is not screened or weakened by a medium, so pouring in a liquid of any specific gravity whatever changes nothing and the force is still \(F\). Matches option A.
reviewNote: [RESOLVED — a second, independent blind derivation reached the printed key (A) without seeing it or the earlier objection, so the key stands. Basis: Newton's law of gravitation contains only the two masses, the separation and G. Unlike the electrostatic force, which is reduced by a factor equal to the dielectric constant of the medium, the gravitational force is not screened by any intervening medium, so filling the space with a liquid of specific gravity 3 leaves it at F. The distractors F/3, F/9 and 3F are the electrostatic analogy carried over wrongly. A.]

subject: Biology
stem: Beri-Beri is caused due to lack of which of the following types of nutrients?
solution: Beri-beri is the deficiency disease of thiamine, which is vitamin \(\mathrm{B}_1\). Thiamine is needed to release energy from carbohydrate, and without it the nerves and the heart muscle suffer, producing the weakness, numbness of the limbs and swelling that mark the disease. It is commonest where polished rice is the staple food, because the thiamine lies in the bran layer that polishing strips away. Thiamine is a vitamin, not a fat, a mineral or water, so the nutrient lacking is a vitamin. Matches option C.

subject: Physics
stem: Which of the following represents voltage?
solution: Potential difference is defined as the work done in carrying unit charge from one point to the other, that is \(V = W/Q\). The charge that flows is itself the current multiplied by the time for which it flows, \(Q = It\). Substituting gives \(V = W/(It)\), which is the work done divided by the product of current and time. Checking the units confirms it: joule divided by ampere-second is joule per coulomb, which is the volt. None of the other combinations reduces to joule per coulomb, since multiplying work by charge gives joule-coulomb, and work multiplied by time and divided by current gives joule-second per ampere. Matches option A.
reviewNote: V = W/Q and Q = I times t, so V = work done divided by (current times time) = A.

subject: Physics
subtopic: Refraction, Speed of Light and TIR
stem: A light wave has frequency of 4 × 1014 Hz and a wavelength of 5 × 10−7 meters in a medium. The refractive index of the medium is:
solution: The speed of the wave in the medium follows from \(v = f\lambda\), so \(v = (4 \times 10^{14})(5 \times 10^{-7}) = 2 \times 10^{8}\) metre per second. The refractive index of a medium is the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum to its speed in that medium, so \(n = c/v = (3 \times 10^{8})/(2 \times 10^{8}) = 1.5\). Note that the frequency is the same in the medium as in vacuum; it is the wavelength and the speed that change. Matches option A.
reviewNote: [RESOLVED — a second, independent blind derivation reached the printed key (A) without seeing it or the earlier objection, so the key stands. Basis: Speed in the medium v = f times lambda = (4e14)(5e-7) = 2e8 m/s. Refractive index n = c/v = 3e8/2e8 = 1.5. A. (Option B 1.33 is water's index, a distractor; option D is less than one, impossible for a material medium.)]

subject: Biology
stem: Due to accumulation of which one of the following, joggers experience pain in their leg muscles after running?
solution: During hard running the muscles demand energy faster than the blood can supply oxygen, so part of the glucose is broken down anaerobically. This incomplete breakdown stops at pyruvic acid, which is then converted to lactic acid instead of being oxidised fully to carbon dioxide and water. The lactic acid collects in the muscle fibres and is what produces the cramp and soreness the runner feels; once oxygen is available again during rest it is cleared and the pain fades. Acetic acid is the acid of vinegar, malic acid occurs in apples and citric acid in lemons and oranges, and none of these accumulates in working muscle. Matches option A.

subject: Physics
stem: Hydrogen bomb is based on the principle of:
solution: A hydrogen bomb works by forcing light nuclei, the hydrogen isotopes deuterium and tritium, to join together into helium; the small amount of mass lost in the process appears as an enormous amount of energy. Such fusion needs temperatures of millions of degrees to overcome the repulsion between the nuclei, which is why an ordinary fission bomb is used as the trigger to supply that heat. Once started, the reaction is allowed to run right through in a fraction of a second with nothing to slow it down, so it is an uncontrolled fusion reaction. Controlled fusion is the aim of a future fusion reactor, while fission, controlled in a nuclear reactor and uncontrolled in an atom bomb, is a different process altogether. Matches option B.
reviewNote: Dedup verdict was "maybe": overlaps live bank row 4565da2c-7203-4a43-ad71-fb62160d95f6 ("Which of the following is based on the principle of nuclear fusion?"). Filed as new because the mock adds the controlled-versus-uncontrolled dimension.

subject: Physics
stem: Consider the following statements about Insulators. (1) Insulators are poor conductors of electricity. (2) Both metals and non- metals are insulators. (3) They have tightly bound electrons. Which of the following is correct?
solution: Statement (1) is correct: an insulator offers an extremely high resistance and so conducts electricity very poorly. Statement (3) is correct as well, and it is the reason for statement (1): in an insulator the valence electrons are held tightly in their bonds, hardly any are free to drift, and the energy gap between the valence band and the conduction band is large. Statement (2) is wrong: a metal has a sea of loosely held free electrons, which is precisely why metals are good conductors and never insulators. Insulators are found only among non-metals and their compounds. So the first and third statements are correct and the second is not. Matches option C.
reviewNote: Rule 1: the three parenthesised statements are flattened into one line. Derivation: (1) and (3) true; (2) false - metals are conductors. So (1) and (3) = C.

subject: Biology
stem: Which of the following are the possible blood groups of the offspring of the parents with blood group O and AB?
solution: The parent of blood group O has the genotype ii and so can pass on only the allele i. The parent of blood group AB has the genotype \(\mathrm{I}^A\mathrm{I}^B\) and can pass on either \(\mathrm{I}^A\) or \(\mathrm{I}^B\). Combining these, every child must be either \(\mathrm{I}^A i\) or \(\mathrm{I}^B i\), and the two are equally likely. Since \(\mathrm{I}^A\) and \(\mathrm{I}^B\) are each dominant over i, these genotypes show as blood group A and blood group B respectively. No child can be O, because that would need i from both parents and the AB parent has none to give, and none can be AB, because that would need both \(\mathrm{I}^A\) and \(\mathrm{I}^B\) and the O parent has neither. Matches option B.
reviewNote: O (ii) crossed with AB (I-A I-B) gives I-A i and I-B i only, so A and B = B.

subject: Physics
stem: Thermometer A and B have ice point marked at 25° and 25° and steam points at 75° and 125° respectively. When thermometer A measures the temperature of a bath as 60°, the reading of B for the same bath is:
solution: Both scales are linear, so the fraction of the way from the ice point to the steam point is the same number on either thermometer, whatever numbers happen to be printed on them. On thermometer A the ice point is 25 and the steam point 75, so the whole interval is \(75 - 25 = 50\) divisions. The reading 60 lies \(60 - 25 = 35\) divisions above its ice point, which is a fraction \(35/50 = 0.7\) of the interval, corresponding to 70 degrees celsius. On thermometer B the ice point is 25 and the steam point 125, so its interval is \(125 - 25 = 100\) divisions. The same fraction of that interval is \(0.7 \times 100 = 70\) divisions, measured again from its own ice point, so the reading is \(25 + 70 = 95\). Matches option D.
reviewNote: Derivation: A reads 60 on a 25-75 scale, a fraction of (60-25)/(75-25) = 0.7; on the 25-125 scale of B that is 25 + 0.7 times 100 = 95 = D.

subject: Physics
stem: In which one of the following cases Ohm’s law is not valid?
solution: Ohm's law states that the current through a conductor is proportional to the potential difference across it, so a graph of V against I must be a straight line through the origin and the resistance must not depend on the size or the sign of V. A wire-bound resistor and the wire of a potentiometer are plain metallic conductors and satisfy this so long as the temperature is steady. A filament lamp does give a curved graph, but only because the filament heats up as the current rises and the resistance of the metal increases with temperature; at any one fixed temperature the filament is still ohmic, so the departure is an indirect one. A junction diode is different in kind. Its V-I graph is curved even at constant temperature, and it is not symmetric either: the same voltage applied in the forward and in the reverse direction produces utterly different currents, so the current is not proportional to the voltage in any sense. Ohm's law fails outright for it. Matches option C.

subject: Chemistry
stem: What is the percentage of lead in lead pencil?
solution: A pencil lead contains no lead at all. It is made of graphite, one of the forms of carbon, mixed with clay and then baked, the proportion of clay deciding how hard or soft the pencil writes. The name is a historical accident: when the graphite deposit at Borrowdale in England was found in the sixteenth century the soft black mineral was mistaken for a form of lead and called plumbago, or black lead, and the name stuck long after the chemistry was understood. So the percentage of lead present is nil. Matches option A.

subject: Physics
stem: If the earth suddenly shrinks (without changing mass) to half of its present radius, the acceleration due to gravity will be at that place:
solution: At the surface of a body of mass \(M\) and radius \(R\) the acceleration due to gravity is \(g = GM/R^{2}\). The mass is stated to be unchanged and only the radius changes, becoming \(R/2\). Substituting, the new value is \(g' = GM/(R/2)^{2} = 4GM/R^{2}\), which is four times the original value. Halving the radius therefore quadruples g, because g varies as the inverse square of the radius. Matches option B.
reviewNote: [RESOLVED — a second, independent blind derivation reached the printed key (B) without seeing it or the earlier objection, so the key stands. Basis: On the surface g = GM/R squared. Mass is held fixed and R is halved, so g' = GM/(R/2) squared = 4GM/R squared = 4g. B. (Under the stored fraction convention 'g 2' is g/2 and 'g 4' is g/4, so B is the only option reading as four times g.)]
